summary: Defines the format of URIs for designating connections and destinations in the Java Message Service. They are for any place a JMS connection needs describing. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A web-address style way to name a message mailbox in Java messaging systems.

questions: how do you reference a jms destination
subtitle: A URI scheme for naming message queues and topics in Java applications.

tldr.problem: Java applications need a standard way to identify and connect to message destinations in the Java Message Service (JMS), and a uniform notation for specifying connection details.
tldr.mechanism: The scheme defines URIs starting with 'jms:', followed by a variant (like 'jndi', 'queue', or 'topic') and the destination name, with optional parameters for routing, priority, and delivery settings.
tldr.outcome: Applications using JMS can reference message destinations in a vendor-neutral way, though the specific behavior depends on the JMS implementation and environment configuration.

today: RFC 6167 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It describes a practical URI scheme in use by Java Message Service implementations and related frameworks for identifying message destinations.

sections.title: What Is a JMS URI
sections.content:
RFC 6167 defines a URI scheme for the Java Message Service (JMS), which is a Java API that lets programs send messages to each other. A JMS URI is a text address like a web URL that identifies a message destination—either a queue (where one program sends and another receives) or a topic (where many programs listen to the same messages)—along with settings about how the message should be sent.

The scheme starts with jms: to mark it as a JMS address. Unlike most URI schemes, it does not map to a single network protocol. Instead, it relies on the JMS API and the Java environment, so two applications need to agree on which JMS provider they use to interoperate.
sections.eli5: A JMS URI is a text address for a message mailbox in Java. It tells the Java system which mailbox to use and how to send the message there.

sections.title: URI Syntax and Structure
sections.content:
A JMS URI has three required parts. It begins with jms:, followed by a variant (such as jndi, queue, or topic), then a colon and the destination name. For example, jms:queue:OrderQueue names a queue called OrderQueue.

After the destination name, optional parameters can be added using query syntax with ? and & separators, just like a web URL. These parameters control delivery options: deliveryMode (whether the message is persistent), timeToLive (how long before the message expires, in milliseconds), priority (a number from 0 to 9), and replyToName (where to send a response). Additional variant-specific or vendor-defined parameters can also be included.
sections.eli5: The address has three parts: the prefix jms:, the type of mailbox (like queue), and the name of the mailbox. You can add settings at the end, separated by ? and &, to control when the message expires or how urgent it is.

sections.title: The Three Variants
sections.content:
RFC 6167 defines three standard variants for locating a message destination. The jndi variant is the most portable: it uses Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) to look up the destination by name in a directory. A URI like jms:jndi:OrderQueue?jndiInitialContextFactory=com.example.Factory tells the application to use JNDI to find a destination called OrderQueue.

The queue and topic variants use the JMS Session API directly, where Session.createQueue(name) and Session.createTopic(name) create a reference to a destination. These variants are simpler but vendor-specific: a queue name from one JMS provider might not work on another. The RFC notes that a JMS URI using these variants might need to be regenerated if switching vendors.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to find a mailbox. The JNDI way is like looking it up in a phone book. The queue and topic ways are like telling the system the mailbox name directly, but they only work with the system that gave you that name.

sections.title: Security Concerns and Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC warns against including sensitive information such as passwords or authentication tokens in a JMS URI, since the URI might be logged, cached, or intercepted. Message senders should be careful not to duplicate critical parameters in both the URI and the actual JMS message, because a malicious actor could craft a URI with parameters that differ from the message itself, leading to inconsistent behavior.

When using configuration parameters like jndiURL or jndiConnectionFactoryName, an attacker who intercepts and modifies these could reroute messages to a third party. Applications should only use these parameters if they trust the source of the URI. Additionally, because JMS URIs can use vendor-specific destination names, a small character change (possibly by homograph substitution using similar-looking characters from different languages) could redirect a message to an unintended destination.
sections.eli5: Be careful not to put passwords in a URI where it might be seen. Also check that the mailbox address is the one you expect, because someone could change a single character to trick your message into going to the wrong place.

sections.title: Use and Registration
sections.content:
JMS URIs are used in messaging applications and frameworks that work with the Java Message Service API. The Service Component Architecture (SCA) specification and SOAP-over-JMS implementations employ this scheme. The scheme is registered with IANA, and vendors can define additional variants for their specific JMS products by registering them under the vnd. prefix (for example, vnd.activemq.queue).

The RFC is Informational, meaning it documents a practical standard that has community support but is not a mandatory Internet standard. It allows flexibility: new variants can be registered, and shared parameters (like delivery mode and priority) maintain the same meaning across all variants for consistency.
sections.eli5: Real Java messaging systems use these URIs, and vendors can add their own types of mailbox by registering them with IANA. The scheme is documented for reference but not a strict requirement.
